title: The Art of Happiness at Work
author: Dalai Lama XIV
review:
Recommended By: Saw it on a library shelf in the spiritual section, intrigued by the title.

5-ish Sentence Summary: Lots of people are dissatisfied by work. Nearly everyone works, and it's a complex topic that is wrapped up in money, interacting with others, identity, ethics, and how we spend our time. Psychiatrist Howard Cutler interviews the Dalai Lama on these topics and intersperses it with his own thoughts, stories, and references. Everything is nuanced, try to be kind.

Roman's Take: I'm not so sure what I wanted out of this book, but it wasn't really.. this. Cutler's writing is cliche, his anecdotes weren't well-integrated, and his ideas felt unfinished. I enjoyed reading the Dalai Lama's thoughts, but I had to wade through a lot of this book to get a few nuggets. Zero for two this year for me on transcribed/edited interviews as books.

Recommended For: I'm not sure I'd recommend it to anyone? For philosophy at work, maybe check out Oliver Burkeman. For learning about Buddhism, I'd instead recommend Bhante Gunaratana (accessible), Bhikku Bodhi (technical), Jack Kornfield or Sharon Salzberg (Western) or Jon Kabat-Zinn (secular.

title: The Power of Myth
author: Bill Moyers Joseph Campbell
review:
Recommended By: Saw it at a book sale/Popular read. Was looking to read something to integrate ideas around ritual/ceremony and meaning in the face of abundant information.

5-ish Sentence Summary: A transcribed extended interview with Joseph Campbell on the history of myths and rituals in various human societies. Myths and rituals help us understand what it means to be human, what is means to be an adult, what it means to live in a society (at large or in particular). We've lost some myths in the modern era, and their replacements don't necessarily do a good job of serving those purposes. The hero's journey (struggle, transformation) is a myth across all societies. Myths are always about the metaphor and what they mean to our own lives

Roman's Take: This book started out amazing, striking, profound. And then a little bit redundant, unfounded, and somewhat -phobic. I think this could have read better if it was not a transcription of an interview because I kept reading Campbell as arrogant while interrupting or disregarding Moyers, but I'm sure it felt different in live dialogue. I really appreciate Campbell's wide knowledge however, he's certainly a prime example of a Generalist at work. 2.5-stars for most of the book but 5-stars for the first third.

Recommended For: A survey of different ancient cultures. A refutation or counterbalance to today's frenetic knowledge management. Not recommended if the topic doesn't already interest you from the get-go, there's probably better works out there for an introduction.

title: Waking Up: A Guide to Spirituality Without Religion
author: Sam Harris
review:
5-ish Sentence Summary
The human mind transcends all possible attempts to understand it. Sam Harris has done a lot of spiritual work. The field of neuroscience is still new and unfolding. Drugs can be pretty great. Religions can be pretty damaging.

My Take
Some people don't appreciate The Beatles when they first hear them, because they sound like so many other bands today. What's underappreciated is that The Beatles were often the first to innovate those sounds, and that the other great bands were simply inspired by the songs of the Beatles. I feel like that's my situation with this book. Meditation, psychedelics, and spirituality without religion are all well-covered topics that have each gone through their own media cycle in popular culture by the time of my reading in 2024. But I suspect some of this was new territory for more people in 2014. So when one of my favorite literary bloggers, Maria Popova, blurbed the cover with "an extraordinary and ambitious masterwork", I hope that I'm just the kid that likes Tame Impala and doesn't think Sgt. Pepper's is anything new.

Recommended For:
- An introduction to meditation
- Ideas on secular uses of psychedelics for spirituality

title: Buddhist Ethics: A Very Short Introduction
author: Damien Keown
review: Great book that assumes understanding of the introductory Buddhist concepts (four noble truths, eight-fold path) so it can focuses on applying them to modern ethical questions. Interesting sections on animal rights, lgbtqia+, euthanasia, and war. Helpful in remembering that Buddhism is comprised of humans, and human's aren't perfect, and there is no perfect contemplative system.

title: The Body
author: Bill Bryson
review:
5-ish Sentence Summary:
Woah, the body is pretty crazy right? Each component is in itself a dynamic and complex system. You know what else is crazy? All the people who have studied the body and the way humans have learned (and been wrong) about these vessels.

Roman's Take:
Like A Short History of Nearly Everything, I enjoy Bill Bryson's style -- everything about him represents his dual American-British citizenship (humor, accent, spellings). I wish I got more about how the body works: the purpose of the organs, how they function, etc. and less about the history of medical science. But I should have expected that since that's Bryson's bread and butter.

Recommended if you:
- Enjoy British witticisms.
- Want to know about crazy shit people did in the past
- Need a lay of the land of the basics of the human body, like me

Not recommended if you:
- Are looking for something beyond Anatomy and Biology 101
- Don't like historical tangents

title: Analog
author: Robert Hassan
review: Interesting and thought-provoking ideas, especially in redefining what "analog" even means besides "non-digital". Most of the ideas after that were technological determinism, re-spun. Some weak arguments at the end, including that the rise of automation in the workplace explains the obesity epidemic (?).
